facts.statement: Jainosaurus lived in India and wider Asia during the Maastrichtian stage, approximately 68 million years ago.
facts.quote: Jainosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur of India and wider Asia, which lived in the Maastrichtian (approximately 68 million years ago).

facts.statement: Jainosaurus is estimated to have been about 18 meters long and weighed 15 metric tons.
facts.quote: It is thought to have been about the same size as its contemporary relative Isisaurus, measuring 18 m long and weighing 15 MT.

facts.statement: The humerus of the type specimen of Jainosaurus measures 134 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The humerus of the type specimen is 134 centimetres long.

facts.statement: The first remains attributed to Jainosaurus, a humerus, were discovered in 1871 or 1872 by Henry Benedict Medlicott.
facts.quote: The first known remains attributable to Jainosaurus, the humerus GSI K22/754, was discovered in 1871 or 1872 by Henry Benedict Medlicott

facts.statement: The holotype remains were found by Charles Alfred Matley between 1917 and 1920 near Jabalpur in the Lameta Formation.
facts.quote: the holotype remains were found by Charles Alfred Matley between 1917 and 1920 near Jabalpur in the Lameta Formation.

facts.statement: The species was originally named Antarctosaurus septentrionalis by Friedrich von Huene and Matley in 1933.
facts.quote: These were named Antarctosaurus septentrionalis by Friedrich von Huene and Matley in 1933.

facts.statement: In 1995, Hunt et al. established the genus Jainosaurus for the species Antarctosaurus septentrionalis, believing it belonged to Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: In 1995 Hunt et al., believing Antarctosaurus to belong to Dicraeosauridae, made the clearly titanosaurian Antarctosaurus septentrionalis the type species of a new genus, Jainosaurus

facts.statement: In 2009, Jeffrey Wilson and others confirmed the validity of Jainosaurus septentrionalis after a detailed reassessment.
facts.quote: In 2009, Jeffrey Wilson and others made a detailed reassessment of Jainosaurus septentrionalis and confirmed its validity.

facts.statement: Postcranial remains previously thought to be lost were found in the collection of the Geological Survey of India in Calcutta.
facts.quote: The postcrania, which had been assumed lost, were shown to be largely present in the collection of the Geological Survey of India at Calcutta.

facts.statement: Wilson and colleagues concluded that Jainosaurus is a valid taxon distinct from Isisaurus.
facts.quote: Wilson e.a. concluded that Jainosaurus is a valid taxon, clearly distinguishable from Isisaurus.

facts.statement: Jainosaurus belongs to the parent group Lithostrotia.
As a large quadrupedal herbivore, an adult Jainosaurus would have measured about 18 meters in length and held its head 6 meters off the ground.
facts.quote: Un gran cuadrúpedo herbívoro , un Jainosaurus adulto habría medido alrededor de 18 metros de largo y sostenía su cabeza a 6 metros de altura.

facts.statement: The generic name Jainosaurus honors the Indian paleontologist Sohan Lal Jain, who studied cranial nerve impressions and published results in 1982.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico honra al paleontólogo indio Sohan Lal Jain, que trabajó en las impresiones de los nervios craneales en el cráneo y en 1982 publicó un estudio sobre los resultados.

facts.statement: Wilson and Upchurch rejected the synonymy of Jainosaurus and Titanosaurus in 2003 due to the dubious status of the latter.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, Wilson y Upchurch en 2003 rechazaron la sinonimia de Jainosaurus y Titanosaurus debido al dudoso estado de este último.

rejected.statement: Jainosaurus is considered a derived member of the Titanosauria, more closely related to South American forms like Pitekunsaurus and Antarctosaurus than to Isisaurus or Rapetosaurus.
rejected.quote: It would have been a fairly derived member of the Titanosauria, more closely related to South American forms like Pitekunsaurus, Muyelensaurus and Antarctosaurus than to Isisaurus or Rapetosaurus.
